content: The film Unnecessary Fuss was created by Ingrid Newkirk and Alex Pacheco of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA). It contains footage recorded by researchers at the University of Pennsylvania's Head Injury Clinic in Philadelphia during 1983-1984. The footage shows experiments in which brain injuries were inflicted on baboons using a hydraulic device. These experiments were part of a research project aimed at studying head injuries caused by car accidents and sports-related trauma. The researchers themselves filmed the procedures, which included scenes of them laughing at the baboons as the injuries were inflicted. In May 1984, the Animal Liberation Front (ALF) raided the laboratory and removed 60 hours of audio and video recordings. These recordings were handed over to PETA, which edited them into a 26-minute film with a voice-over by Newkirk. The film was distributed to the media and Congress, leading to significant public backlash. As a result, the laboratory was shut down, the chief veterinarian was dismissed, and the university was placed on probation. The title of the film, Unnecessary Fuss, was derived from a comment made by the clinic's head, Dr. Thomas Gennarelli, who had previously dismissed concerns about his research as having the potential to cause unnecessary fuss. The film depicts at least one sedated but not fully anesthetized baboon restrained on an operating table. The animal's shaved head was secured with dental cement inside a helmet. A hydraulic device, referred to as Penn 2, delivered a force of up to 1,000 g to the baboon's head, simulating whiplash by pushing the head forward at a 60-degree angle. After the injury, the baboon's head was forcibly removed from the helmet using a hammer and screwdriver. In one instance, part of the baboon's ear was torn off along with the helmet. A researcher was heard laughing and making comments such as, It's a boy, and Looks like I left a little ear behind. The footage also shows researchers laughing at the injured animals, performing electrocautery on a seemingly conscious baboon, smoking during surgical procedures, and playing loud music while the animals were being injured. In one scene, a severely injured baboon was held up to the camera while researchers mocked it, saying things like, Don't be shy now, sir, nothing to be afraid of, followed by laughter. Another scene showed a brain-damaged, drooling monkey strapped into a high chair, with researchers making sarcastic comments about the animal's condition. One researcher was heard saying, You better hope the anti-vivisection people don't get ahold of this film. The University of Pennsylvania responded to the film by claiming it was a caricature of the events in the laboratory. Before the release of the footage, Dr. Thomas Langfitt, the chief investigator at the Head Injury Clinic, denied any abuse had occurred. He stated that the animals were treated humanely and that researchers would never laugh at the baboons, asserting that they were treated with the same respect as human patients. However, an investigation by 18 veterinarians from the American College of Laboratory Animal Medicine, commissioned by the Office for Protection from Research Risks (OPRR), found serious violations in the clinic. These violations included questionable levels of anesthesia, lack of veterinary oversight before and after surgeries, failure to maintain aseptic conditions during survival surgeries, improper cleaning of the operating theater, and smoking in the presence of oxygen tanks. The investigation also uncovered deficiencies in other laboratories at the university. As a result, the university's chief veterinarian was fired, new training programs were implemented, and the university was placed on probation, requiring quarterly progress reports to the OPRR. Critics of the PETA film pointed out that it was heavily edited, which led to misrepresentations. Initially, the OPRR refused to investigate the allegations because PETA had not released the unedited footage. When the full 60 hours of recordings were eventually provided, the OPRR found that the scenes of brain damage being inflicted involved only one baboon, despite the film giving the impression that multiple animals were subjected to the same treatment. The OPRR identified 25 inaccuracies in Newkirk's voice-over commentary. For example, a water spill over a conscious baboon during surgery was misidentified by both a clinic researcher and Newkirk as an acid spill.
